query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy nanoparticles, tailoring the mix of constituent metals to maximize local chemical fluctuations—especially by incorporating elements with large differences in electronegativity and atomic mass—induces lattice strain that hinders atomic diffusion. This suppression of diffusion maintains the solid solution phase (and thus both structural and chemical stability) over the broad operating window of 473–1923 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Design two compositions: one where metals are chosen to maximize differences in electronegativity and atomic mass (to enhance local strain and chemical fluctuations) and a control composition with metals displaying more similar properties.
generation.conditions: Operating conditions simulating catalytic and thermoelectric applications, with temperature ranges spanning from 473 K to 1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice strain generated by local chemical fluctuations arising from significant electronegativity and mass differences among constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: The induced local lattice distortions disrupt long-range atomic order and slow down atomic diffusion, preventing phase segregation or structural transitions at elevated temperatures. This mechanism is similar to observations in high-entropy thermoelectric materials where bond fluctuations from electronegativity differences contribute to reduced lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered with higher electronegativity and mass differences will exhibit lower rates of atomic diffusion and a maintained single-phase solid solution even at 1923 K, compared to control samples. This should correlate with stable catalytic and thermoelectric performances over the test temperature range.
generation.baseline: High-entropy nanoparticles in which the constituent metals have relatively similar electronegativity and mass, leading to minimal local chemical fluctuation and less induced lattice strain.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to hold primarily within the examined 473–1923 K range and under controlled catalytic/thermoelectric reaction conditions. Outside these temperature windows, or in environments that promote alternative reactive processes, the influence of engineered local chemical fluctuations might be less significant or even detrimental.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thresholds for the required differences in electronegativity and mass that optimize stabilization are not fully defined, and other factors (like atomic radius differences) may also contribute. Quantitative contributions from each parameter remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoparticles: one engineered with high differences in electronegativity and mass between metals and a control set with metals having similar properties. Subject both sets to an in situ high-temperature treatment from 473 K to 1923 K under conditions representative of catalytic/thermoelectric operation. Monitor phase integrity using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and atomic-level structure using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with elemental mapping.
measurements: Phase composition over time (via in situ XRD)
Atomic diffusion rates and local chemical fluctuation (via TEM and chemical mapping)
Relevant performance indicators (e.g., catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced electronegativity/mass differences do not display significantly lower atomic diffusion rates and fail to maintain a single-phase solid solution compared to the control nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that intensified local chemical fluctuations stabilize the structure (via diffusion suppression) is falsified.

## Abstract
In high-entropy materials, local chemical fluctuation from multiple elements inhabiting the same crystallographic site plays a crucial role in their unique properties. Using atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identified the respective contributions of different element characteristics on the local chemical fluctuation of high-entropy structures in thermoelectric materials. Electronegativity and mass had a comparable influence on the fluctuations of constituent elements, while the radius made a slight contribution. The local chemical fluctuation was further tailored by selecting specific elements to induce large lattice distortion and strong strain fluctuation to lower lattice thermal conductivity independent of increased entropy. The chemical bond fluctuation induced by the electronegativity difference had a noticeable contribution to the composition-dependent lattice thermal conductivity in addition to the known fluctuations of mass and strain field. Our findings provide a fundamental principle for tuning local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials. However, the low performance and conversion efficiency of thermoelectric materials have hindered their realistic applications. As the latest promising approach (, ), the high-entropy strategy has demonstrated substantial improvements in the performance of thermoelectric materials (, , ). The local chemical fluctuation can interrupt the long-range periodic arrangement of atoms and induce the strong scattering of heat-carrying phonons (), which largely reduce the lattice thermal conductivity and improves thermoelectric properties. The vast number of possible element combinations in the high-entropy strategy offers an enormous amount of space to tune local chemical fluctuation. However, altering the composition of high-entropy materials may not always lead to desired properties, and the tailoring of local chemical fluctuations by constituent elements has remained unclear in most of studies.
